checkpoints: Cơ chế TÍNH cache key (hash từ parent layer + instruction + checksum COPY/ADD) giống hệt nhau ở cả hai môi trường — đây KHÔNG phải bug do cache bị invalidate sai như vấn đề thứ tự COPY.
Backend cache MẶC ĐỊNH của BuildKit là "local" — lưu trực tiếp trên disk của máy đang build, cụ thể tại `~/.docker/buildx/`.
Trên máy local, đó là MỘT disk duy nhất tồn tại xuyên suốt nhiều lần build, nên cache của lần build trước "sống sót" đến lần build kế tiếp — đó là lý do thấy `CACHED`.

Trên GitHub Actions, mỗi lần chạy workflow nhận một runner ảo hóa HOÀN TOÀN MỚI, được cấp phát rồi hủy ngay sau khi job xong — disk local của runner đó (và cache trên đó) biến mất hoàn toàn sau mỗi lần chạy.

Hệ quả: cache của lần chạy trước nằm trên một runner không còn tồn tại nên build kế tiếp (trên runner mới khác) không thể tìm lại được — build luôn chậm như lần đầu dù `package.json` không đổi, vì về bản chất MỌI lần chạy CI đều là "máy sạch, không cache".

Giải pháp: đưa backend cache ra khỏi vòng đời của runner, đến nơi TỒN TẠI ĐỘC LẬP với runner nào đang chạy — dùng `docker buildx build --cache-to=type=registry,ref=<registry>/<image>:cache,mode=max` để ĐẨY toàn bộ cache (kể cả layer trung gian) lên registry OCI ngay sau khi build, và `--cache-from=type=registry,ref=<registry>/<image>:cache` ở lần build sau để KÉO cache đó về trước khi build.

Nếu dùng riêng GitHub Actions, có backend tiện hơn — `--cache-to=type=gha`/`--cache-from=type=gha` — dùng trực tiếp dịch vụ cache của GitHub Actions (có quota miễn phí theo repo), không cần tự quản một registry cache riêng.

Áp dụng đúng pattern này thường nâng tỉ lệ cache hit của CI từ khoảng 20% (mọi lần chạy đều bị coi là build sạch, tình trạng hiện tại) lên 80-95%, vì cache giờ được CHIA SẺ giữa các lần chạy job khác nhau, không còn phụ thuộc việc job đó "may mắn" rơi đúng runner đã build lần trước.
Điểm sai trong lý luận của đồng nghiệp: "token chỉ dùng lúc build, không có trong final image" nhầm lẫn giữa runtime image (đúng là sạch, không có .npmrc) với toàn bộ bề mặt có thể bị lộ.

ARG/--build-arg ghi giá trị token vào image history (layer metadata) của builder stage một cách VĨNH VIỄN, ngay cả khi RUN sau đó xoá file .npmrc trong cùng lệnh — xoá file chỉ xoá nội dung khỏi filesystem layer, không xoá được record trong history.

Bất kỳ ai có quyền pull/inspect builder stage đều có thể đọc được giá trị NPM_TOKEN qua `docker history --no-trunc` hoặc `docker inspect`, kể cả khi runtime image hoàn toàn sạch — đây chính là bề mặt lộ thật sự, không phải ở runtime image cuối cùng.
Rủi ro càng nghiêm trọng nếu builder stage được push lên registry cache (`--cache-to`) hoặc CI build log giữ lại toàn bộ log — token khi đó lộ ra ngoài phạm vi máy build cục bộ.
Cách sửa: bỏ hẳn ARG NPM_TOKEN/--build-arg, thay bằng BuildKit secret mount: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci --omit=dev`.
Secret mount là tmpfs chỉ tồn tại trong đúng thời gian RUN đang thực thi, KHÔNG BAO GIỜ được BuildKit ghi vào layer hay history, nên không cần rm thủ công mà history vẫn sạch tuyệt đối.
Build command tương ứng: `docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=$HOME/.npmrc-token -t myapp .` (đọc token từ file tạm) hoặc `--secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN` (đọc trực tiếp từ biến môi trường).

Sau khi sửa, verify bằng `docker history --no-trunc myapp` (và cả builder stage trung gian nếu build riêng) để xác nhận không còn dòng nào chứa giá trị token — đây là pattern an toàn duy nhất cho npm token, SSH key hay bất kỳ credential nào cần trong lúc build.

Root cause: the key-based approach uses a shared, static private key that is not bound to any specific identity, so any engineer with read access to the secret manager can sign on the pipeline's behalf, and there is no way to audit who actually signed a given image — violating both requirements (1) and (2).

Solution direction: switch to cosign keyless signing, where CI generates an ephemeral ECDSA keypair that exists only in the job's RAM and obtains an OIDC token representing the specific workflow's identity rather than a generic shared account.
Fulcio CA verifies the OIDC token and public key, then issues a short-lived (~10 minute) x509 certificate whose SAN is bound to the exact workflow identity (e.g. the specific repo/workflow/branch).
Cosign uses the ephemeral private key to sign the image digest, pushes the signature and certificate to the registry, and writes an entry to Rekor — a public, immutable transparency log.
This satisfies requirement (1): it is known exactly which workflow signed a given image, rather than guessing from a shared key.

This satisfies requirement (2): there is no static private key left to steal, since signing requires a valid OIDC token from the exact right identity provider for the exact right workflow — registry read access alone can no longer let someone sneak-sign.

For requirement (3), install an admission controller (Kyverno or cosign policy-controller) on Kubernetes with a ClusterImagePolicy specifying the OIDC issuer and a subjectRegExp matching only the allowed workflow/branch, so any Pod referencing an image signed by a non-matching workflow is rejected at the control plane automatically.

Trade-off: Rekor's public nature means every entry (signer's OIDC email, image digest) is publicly visible, which can leak sensitive metadata like an unannounced product name or release timing; if privacy matters more than public auditability, the alternatives are self-hosting the entire Sigstore stack (private Fulcio + Rekor) or reverting to key-based signing via a cloud KMS with IAM-based audit logging (losing Rekor's public transparency) — neither option is free, so it must be weighed against how sensitive the product actually is.

Multi-stage Dockerfile: a builder stage using `golang:1.22` compiles the Go binary, and a separate, minimal runtime stage copies out only the compiled binary (not the source, toolchain, or module cache).

The build uses `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build` to produce a STATIC binary — one with no dependency on any dynamic C library (glibc/musl) at runtime — which is the prerequisite for running on an absolutely minimal base image.
The runtime stage uses `FROM scratch` rather than `distroless` or `alpine`, since the Go binary is already fully static and needs no libc at all.
`scratch` is an absolutely EMPTY image (0 layers, 0 bytes beyond what you copy in), giving a final image just a few MB (the binary's size) with almost no CVEs from the OS, since there is no OS.

Because `scratch` has nothing at all, CA certificates must be manually added by copying `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` from the builder stage (where the `golang:1.22` Debian base already has it) into the runtime image.

CA certificates are needed because the Go runtime must verify the target server's certificate chain for outbound HTTPS calls; skipping this step makes every HTTPS request fail with an error like "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" even though the code is correct.
Similarly, if the app needs timezone handling (e.g. `time.LoadLocation`), tzdata must also be copied in, since `scratch` doesn't include that either.

Because the apiserver itself is suspected of being overloaded, the correct approach is to SSH directly into the node running the Pod and proceed bottom-up per the layer diagram, bypassing kubectl/apiserver entirely rather than depending on the component in question — this is exactly the approach that applies when the apiserver is the suspect, or when `kubectl describe pod` only gives a generic message insufficient to diagnose which layer is actually stuck.
Step 1 (CRI layer): use `crictl` instead of `docker`, since Kubernetes 1.24 removed dockershim and kubelet talks to containerd directly via the CRI gRPC API, making `docker` irrelevant here.
Use `crictl pods | grep <pod-name>` to check the state of the pod sandbox (network namespace + infra container).
Use `crictl ps -a` to check the state of the specific container inside that sandbox (created/running/exited, with exit reason).

`crictl logs <container-id>` reads logs directly from containerd — a path that differs from `kubectl logs` (which must go through kubelet then apiserver) — so it still works even when the apiserver isn't responding.

Step 2: if `crictl` doesn't give enough information about why the container failed to create (e.g. image pull failure, volume mount error), check `journalctl -u containerd -f` — the daemon layer receiving CRI commands from kubelet and coordinating shim/runc, for errors like image pull or snapshot failure — and in parallel `journalctl -u kubelet -f` — the layer above containerd where policy decisions (resource, volume mount requests) happen — reading both since the error could originate from either layer.
Step 3: only if the problem is still suspected at the lowest layer (runc, namespace/cgroup), use `runc list` to see all runc container instances known to it.
Use `runc state <id>` to get the detailed state of the specific stuck container.

restartPolicy: Always is enforced by the kubelet on the node and only governs the container inside a Pod that still exists: on a container crash, the kubelet restarts it in place, the Pod keeps its same name/IP, and the RESTARTS counter increments.
restartPolicy: Always does NOT cover a Pod being deleted or lost along with its node — recreating a missing Pod is a controller's responsibility, not something the kubelet's restart mechanism does.
A bare Pod created via `kubectl run` (no Deployment) has empty ownerReferences — nobody owns or manages it.
When the node goes down, every Pod scheduled on it disappears with it; for a bare Pod that's the end — nothing rebuilds it, regardless of restartPolicy, because it has no controller watching over it.
The fix is to wrap the service in a Deployment, which in turn creates a ReplicaSet to own the Pod.

The ReplicaSet runs a continuous reconcile loop that compares Pods matching its label selector against the desired `replicas` count; when the node restart wipes out the Pod, it detects the shortfall and creates a new Pod (different name/IP) on a surviving node, so the service self-heals without manual intervention.
General rule: bare Pods should only be used for one-off debug purposes (e.g. `kubectl run -it --rm`); every real workload needs a controller (like a Deployment/ReplicaSet) behind it.
Pod IPs are ephemeral — they change on every restart, reschedule, or scale event — so hardcoding/calling a Pod's IP directly is unreliable.
Service assigns a stable ClusterIP (plus a DNS name) that persists for the lifetime of the Service, independent of any individual Pod's IP.
Service continuously builds an Endpoints object from every Ready Pod matching its selector.
kube-proxy on each node DNATs requests sent to the ClusterIP to one of the Pod IPs listed in Endpoints — this DNAT/redirect is the actual load-balancing mechanism.
ClusterIP (the default type) is reachable only from inside the cluster and is used for internal service-to-service calls.

NodePort opens the same static port (in the 30000–32767 range) on every node, used for raw exposure in simple labs/on-prem setups, or as the base layer under an external LB/Ingress (the Ingress controller itself is often exposed this way too).
LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider for a public IP plus an external L4 load balancer dedicated to a single Service — simple, but each Service getting its own IP makes it expensive at scale.

Because of that per-Service cost, production rarely gives every app its own LoadBalancer; instead one Ingress (L7) sits behind one LoadBalancer/entrypoint and routes by host/path to many Services, keeping things cheaper and centralizing TLS/rate-limiting.
startupProbe cấu hình httpGet path=/healthz port=8080 với periodSeconds 5 và failureThreshold 12 (5s × 12 = 60s) — cho app tối đa 60 giây để hoàn tất boot mà không bị coi là fail.

livenessProbe cấu hình httpGet path=/healthz port=8080 với periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 2 (khớp đúng SLA phản hồi dưới 2 giây của app), failureThreshold 3 — sau khi đã ổn định, kiểm tra mỗi 10 giây, phải 3 lần fail liên tiếp (30s) mới bị coi là hang thật và bị restart.

readinessProbe cấu hình httpGet path=/healthz port=8080 với periodSeconds 5, timeoutSeconds 2, failureThreshold 2 — kiểm tra nhanh hơn liveness vì rớt khỏi Endpoints là rủi ro thấp hơn việc restart container, giúp bắt tình trạng 'tạm bận' sớm mà không cần restart.
Cơ chế mấu chốt: chừng nào startupProbe chưa Succeeded thì kubelet KHÔNG chạy livenessProbe/readinessProbe, nên Pod không thể bị kill bởi liveness trong lúc đang boot dù /healthz chưa trả lời được.

Cách tiếp cận này thay thế việc nhét initialDelaySeconds lớn vào liveness — cách cũ vừa cứng nhắc (hỏng nếu boot có lúc lâu hơn dự kiến) vừa làm chậm việc phát hiện hang thật một khi hệ thống đã vào steady-state.

Corrects the misconception directly: Secret is NOT encrypted by default in etcd — it is only base64-encoded, trivially reversible via `base64 -d` by anyone with RBAC read access, so base64 is not encryption.

Explains why the Pod doesn't see new config: env-var-injected values (`valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`/`secretKeyRef` or `envFrom`) are read only ONCE at container startup and stay fixed for the process's whole lifetime — reapplying/editing the source has zero effect on an already-running Pod.
Names at least one genuine Secret-vs-ConfigMap difference beyond encryption: separately tightenable RBAC and/or Secret values not printed by default in `kubectl describe`/logs output.

Contrasts with volume-mounted config: the kubelet auto re-syncs the mounted file whenever the source changes (via the `..data` symlink mechanism, roughly a 1-minute delay), so an app that re-reads the file can pick up updates without a restart.
Notes the specific mechanical detail that Secret is mounted into tmpfs (RAM-backed) rather than written to node disk when consumed as a volume.
States that true safe-at-rest for Secret requires an additional layer beyond the default — enabling etcd encryption-at-rest or using an external KMS/Vault.
Gives the fast remediation for the current env-based case: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<x>` to spin up new Pods that re-read the updated env.
Gives a durable remediation: hash the ConfigMap/Secret content into a Pod template annotation (Helm/Kustomize checksum pattern) so any change auto-changes the hash and triggers a rolling update.
Correctly identifies the STATUS as CreateContainerConfigError and explains it means the Pod was scheduled successfully (node assigned, image present) but the container itself never started.

Correctly contrasts this with CrashLoopBackOff: in CrashLoopBackOff the app process actually starts and then dies repeatedly, whereas CreateContainerConfigError happens before the app process ever runs (during kubelet's container-config prep step).
States that `kubectl get pod` only shows the STATUS as a symptom and that `kubectl describe pod` (specifically its Events section) is needed to find the real underlying cause.

Correctly derives the root cause from the given Events output: the Pod references an env var via `secretKeyRef` pointing at key `NOPE_DOES_NOT_EXIST`, which Secret `app-secret` does not actually contain, so the kubelet cannot assemble the container's environment.

Gives a concrete corrective fix: inspect the Secret's actual keys (e.g. `kubectl get secret app-secret -o jsonpath='{.data}'`) and correct the Pod/Deployment spec to reference the right key name, or add the missing key to the Secret.
Mentions the `optional: true` field on `secretKeyRef` as the correct way to let the Pod start even when that key may legitimately be absent.
Describes verifying the fix by reapplying and confirming `kubectl get pod` reaches `1/1 Running` with no further key-related errors in `kubectl describe pod`.
